text_blocks.snippet: Pericarditis diagnosis involves a combination of clinical evaluation, electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, and potentially other tests like blood work or chest X-ray. A pericardial friction rub, though present in only about 30% of cases, is highly specific for pericarditis.
snippet_highlighted_words: involves a combination of clinical evaluation, electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, and potentially other tests like blood work or chest X-ray

text_blocks.snippet: Here's a breakdown of the diagnostic process:

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Doctors will assess for characteristic symptoms like sharp, stabbing chest pain (often worsened by lying down or breathing deeply), fever, weakness, trouble breathing, and palpitations.

list.title: Physical Examination:
list.snippet: A physical exam might reveal a pericardial friction rub (a scratchy sound heard with a stethoscope), tachycardia, and signs of inflammation. Also, signs of shock (like diaphoresis, clamminess, tachycardia, or decreased blood pressure) may be noted.

list.title: Medical History:
list.snippet: The doctor will also consider the patient's medical history for any conditions that could be related to pericarditis, such as infections, autoimmune diseases, or kidney failure.
ECG is a crucial test as it often shows specific changes in the electrical activity of the heart in pericarditis.
ECG findings suggestive of acute pericarditis include ST-segment elevation (but typically less than 5mm), ST-segment concavity, PR-segment elevation in aVR, and a lack of abnormal Q-waves.
The ECG can also help rule out other conditions like myocardial infarction (heart attack).
An echocardiogram uses sound waves to create images of the heart, allowing doctors to assess how well the heart is pumping and to check for any fluid buildup around the heart (pericardial effusion).
It can help determine if the pericardial inflammation is affecting heart function.

list.title: Blood Tests:
list.snippet: Blood tests can help identify the underlying cause of pericarditis, such as infections, autoimmune conditions, or kidney problems.

list.title: Chest X-ray:
list.snippet: Chest X-rays may reveal cardiomegaly (enlarged heart) or signs of pulmonary edema.

list.title: Cardiac Catheterization:
list.snippet: In cases of constrictive pericarditis, cardiac catheterization can be used to measure pressures in the heart chambers and confirm the diagnosis.

list.title: Cardiac CT or MRI:
list.snippet: These imaging techniques can provide more detailed images of the heart and pericardium, helping to identify inflammation, thickening, or other abnormalities.

list.title: Pericardial Biopsy:
list.snippet: In some cases, a pericardial biopsy might be necessary to determine the cause of pericarditis.
The specific tests used to diagnose pericarditis will vary depending on the patient's individual circumstances and the suspected cause of the condition.
Diagnosis should be made by a qualified healthcare professional (doctor).
Prompt diagnosis and treatment are important to prevent complications, such as cardiac tamponade or constrictive pericarditis.
